summary: Dunne works in Buddhist studies, Tibetology, and philosophy. He studied at Amherst College and Harvard University, including doctoral work under Nagatomi and Eckel. He held posts at Harvard, Lausanne, Emory (~2005–2016), and the University of Wisconsin-Madison (1999, 2015).

Kelly is a scholar in Indology and history and archaeology. He has held appointments at the University of Chicago, attested in 2007 and attested in 2026 as Christian W. Mackauer Professor of Anthropology and of Social Sciences.

Smith is a scholar in Indology, linguistics, and computational studies. He was Lecturer in Sanskrit at SOAS University of London (1975), University Lecturer in Sanskrit at the University of Cambridge (1984), and Professor at Cambridge (2001–2007).

Loori worked in Buddhist studies. He studied at Rutgers University and trained under Soen Nakagawa and Taizan Maezumi. He taught at Naropa University in 1974 and served as Abbot of Zen Mountain Monastery from circa 1980 to 2009.
Buksbazen is a scholar in Buddhist studies and religious studies. He studied at the Zen Center of Los Angeles and under Taizan Maezumi and Bernie Glassman (both attested 2002).

Paterson was an Indologist and historian-archaeologist. A co-founder of The Asiatic Society, he served with the East India Company from 1776 and held an appointment as Judge and Magistrate at the University of Dhaka.

Rees was active in Indology and other fields. After attending Cheltenham College (~1867–1873), he served in the Madras Civil Service (1875), the Indian Civil Service (~1875–1901), and on the Council of India as an Additional Member (1895–1900).

Mayne worked in Indology and law. Educated at Trinity College Dublin, he served as Professor of Law at Presidency College, Chennai (~1857–1872) and Professor of Common Law at the Inns of Court (1880–1885).

DeFrancis was a sinologist and linguist. He studied at Columbia University (~1938–1946) and Yale University (~1942–1943). He later held posts at Seton Hall University (~1961–1966) and the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa (~1966–1976).

Dewey was a philosopher educated at the University of Vermont (~1875–1879) and Johns Hopkins University (~1882–1884). He held academic posts at Michigan (~1884–1894), Minnesota Twin Cities (~1888–1889), Chicago (~1894–1904), and Columbia University (~1904–1930).

Dowson worked in Indology, linguistics, and history and archaeology. He studied under Edwin Norris and served as Professor of Hindustani at University College London (1855–1877) and at Staff College, Camberley (1855–1877).

Drake was an Indologist and religious studies scholar educated at Regent's Park College and the University of Oxford. He served as Vice-Principal and Professor of Theology and Ethics at Serampore College (1910–1926) and at Saharanpur Theological Seminary until 1933.
Bate was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Regent's Park College. He served as a member of the Baptist Missionary Society from 1865 to 1897.

Cort is an Indologist and scholar of religious studies. He completed a BA at the University of Wisconsin-Madison (~1970–1974) and an AM at Harvard University (~1980–1984), and he has served as Professor at Denison University (~1993).

Richards was an Indologist and historian. He studied at the University of New Hampshire (~1957–1961) and UC Berkeley (~1961–1970), holding posts at the University of Wisconsin-Madison (~1968–1977) and Duke University (~1977–2007).

Fleet worked in Indology and history-archaeology. Educated at UCL and under Theodor Goldstücker, he served in the Indian Civil Service (1865–1897), as Government of India Epigraphist (1883–1886), and as Honorary Secretary of the Royal Asiatic Society (1906–1917).
Duthie was a botanist who served as Superintendent of the Saharanpur Botanical Garden from circa 1876 to 1903 and as Director of the Botanical Survey of India from circa 1891 to 1903.

Royle worked in Indology and botany. Educated at Edinburgh and Addiscombe, he was Superintendent at Saharanpur Botanical Garden (1823–1831), Professor of Materia Medica at King's College London (1837–1856), and oversaw the museum of vegetable products at the India Office (~1838–1858).

Youngson worked in linguistics and Indology. He earned an M.A. (~1869–1873) and D.D. (by 1893) from the University of Aberdeen, and served as a missionary with the Church of Scotland from 1875 to 1907.
Browne was an Indologist and linguist. He studied at Exeter College, Oxford (~1853–1854) and the East India Company College (~1854–1856), joining the Bengal Civil Service in 1858.
